name: Prize crossword No 26,764
preamble: Definitions in nine clues lead to solutions (one of two words, one of three, one hyphenated) that are to be entered in the grid with 7 24 16. Their wordplay and indicated lengths refer to the required grid entries.

clue.text: A number of girls live very superficially

indicators.note: what is superficial stays on the surface, so only the outside letters of the word count

blocks.note: to be is to exist or live
the outside letters of 'very'

explanation.surface: A crowd of young women who lead shallow lives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Live' looks like part of the girls' description, but it is a plain verb meaning to exist.
explanation.definitionFit: A bevy is a collective noun for a group, traditionally used of girls or quails.

clue.text: Homosexual couple adopt son, just landed here?

indicators.note: parents who adopt take a newcomer into the family home, so something is taken inside

blocks.note: two men's names, Stan and Ted, as a male couple
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A gay couple adopt a boy, as if the child had just flown in.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'homosexual couple' is a pair of men's first names, with the son between them. Stansted is one of London's airports, so a passenger who has just landed may be there.
explanation.definitionFit: Stansted is a London airport, a place where travellers arrive by plane; the question mark flags definition by example.

clue.text: Sound of gong and fiddle

indicators.note: the sound of a word is how it is said, so we want a word pronounced the same

blocks.note: a gong is British slang for a medal or decoration

explanation.surface: Someone bangs a gong and scrapes a violin together.
explanation.walkthrough: The gong is not a percussion instrument here: in British slang a gong is a medal or honour.
explanation.definitionFit: To fiddle with something is to tamper or interfere with it, which is what meddling means.

clue.text: Sunday get away, taking in a picture

indicators.note: to take something in is to absorb it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for Sunday
to escape is to get away
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Sunday escape that includes a trip to see a film or painting.
explanation.walkthrough: The A goes inside ESCAPE, straight after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A seascape is a painting or drawing of the sea, one particular kind of picture.

clue.text: Fragments making appearance on board vessel

indicators.note: whatever is on board a ship is inside it, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: mien is a person's look or bearing
SS stands for steamship

explanation.surface: Debris turns up on a ship's deck.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leads to SMITHEREENS; the preamble says to enter it with THERE removed, and the wordplay builds that shorter grid entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Smithereens are tiny broken pieces, as when something is smashed to bits.

clue.text: Heavy drinker gets in another round — hence black mark?

indicators.note: getting something in means taking it inside, so the letters are enclosed

blocks.note: a sot is a drunkard
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: A boozer buys one more round of drinks and earns disapproval.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Another round' sounds like drinks at the bar, but it is just the round letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: Soot is black powder from burning, the cause of a dirty black smudge; the question mark admits the indirect definition.

clue.text: Nowhere is unimportant

blocks.note: first meaning: in no place, taken literally
second meaning: the idiom for something irrelevant

explanation.walkthrough: This phrase is also the puzzle's theme: nine answers are entered with HERE or THERE left out.
explanation.definitionFit: Read literally, the phrase means in no place at all; as an idiom it means irrelevant or of no consequence.

clue.text: Particle of iron needing minor change

indicators.note: a change alters the form, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron
taken as written

explanation.surface: A bit of iron that only needs a small adjustment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Particle of iron' reads as a filing, but particle is the definition and iron gives its symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: A fermion is a class of subatomic particle, such as an electron or proton, in physics.

clue.text: Colour associated with Aphrodite

blocks.note: the wordplay half: a greenish-blue colour, which is the grid entry
the definition half: Cytherean, from Cythera, the goddess's island

explanation.surface: A shade linked with the goddess of love.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition gives CYTHEREAN; with THERE removed it is entered as CYAN, which the wordplay half, 'Colour', gives directly.
explanation.definitionFit: Aphrodite was called Cytherea after the island of Cythera, so anything belonging to her is Cytherean.

clue.text: In modest clothing, greetings bursting out

indicators.note: clothing wraps around the wearer, so one set of letters is dressed around the other

blocks.note: decent clothing is modest
his, plural of hi, a greeting

explanation.surface: Someone dressed demurely is suddenly loud with hellos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greetings' gives the plural of hi, two short words read as one.
explanation.definitionFit: In botany, a dehiscent seed pod splits open naturally to release its contents.

clue.text: No agriculturalist, old tribesman diverts great river

indicators.note: to divert is to send off a different way, so the letters take a new course

blocks.note: the Huns were an ancient nomadic people
taken as written
R is the abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: An ancient warrior, not a farmer, changes the course of a big river.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leads to HUNTER-GATHERER; it is entered with THERE removed, and the wordplay spells that grid entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Hunter-gatherers live by foraging and hunting wild food rather than by farming crops or herds.

clue.text: In the dark, guide just terribly defective

indicators.note: something defective is incomplete, so only a broken-off run of letters is used

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words, minus their ends

explanation.surface: A guide working in darkness who is hopelessly bad at it.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition gives USHERETTE, a cinema attendant who shows people to their seats with a torch; it is entered with HERE removed.
explanation.definitionFit: An usherette guides people to their seats in a darkened cinema or theatre auditorium.

clue.text: United male assembly

indicators.note: to assemble is to put parts together, so these letters are put together afresh

blocks.note: U is the abbreviation for United, as in football club names
taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition as well as the wordplay: the ulema is traditionally an all-male body of scholars.
explanation.definitionFit: The ulema is the body of Muslim scholars trained in Islamic law and theology, historically men only.

clue.text: Tight-fisted party — in Britain, the left

blocks.note: near is a British word for stingy
a side is a party in a dispute

explanation.surface: A political party of misers is said to be the British left wing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' and 'the left' suggest politics, but the answer is about cars. Britain drives on the left, so the side nearest the kerb is the left.
explanation.definitionFit: The nearside of a vehicle is the side closest to the kerb, which in British driving is the left.

clue.text: Leaders of domestic football get behind Jeremy's anthem

indicators.note: leaders go in front, so the first letters of the following words are taken

blocks.note: the first letters of these two words
to lag is to fall behind

explanation.surface: Captains of the home football league rally behind a politician's song.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition gives THE RED FLAG, the Labour Party's anthem; Jeremy is Jeremy Corbyn, Labour's leader when this appeared. It is entered with THERE removed.
explanation.definitionFit: The Red Flag is the socialist song traditionally sung at Labour Party conferences, which Corbyn sang with gusto.

clue.text: Like some friends to be given food, including slice of apple

indicators.note: to include is to hold inside, so one piece is placed within another
a slice is a single thin piece, so just one letter is taken, from the front

blocks.note: fed means given food
the first letter of 'apple'

explanation.surface: Pals who are to be fed, an apple slice included.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition gives FEATHERED, since birds are called feathered friends; it is entered with THERE removed.
explanation.definitionFit: Birds are jokingly called our feathered friends, so some friends are described as having plumage.

clue.text: See 7
Extremely desirable fox that is in favour

blocks.note: tod is an old and Scottish word for a fox
i.e. stands for id est, that is; the 'is' doubles as link
for means in favour of

explanation.surface: A very attractive fox wins popular approval.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fox' suggests an attractive person, but it is the animal under its dialect name.
explanation.definitionFit: Something described as to die for is so desirable you would sacrifice anything to have it.

clue.text: One swimming alone?

blocks.note: first meaning: a flatfish
second meaning: single, only

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a lone swimmer; split it and one part is a fish, the other means only.
explanation.definitionFit: The sole is a flatfish that swims in the sea, and sole as an adjective means only or solitary.

clue.text: Most made out knight's winning move

indicators.note: out can mean wrong or not in order, so the letters are put in a different sequence

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Most people worked out how the knight won.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition gives SMOTHERED MATE, a chess term; it is entered with THERE removed, and the wordplay spells that shorter entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A smothered mate is a checkmate delivered by a knight to a king hemmed in by its own pieces.

clue.text: What the Observer does: keep following the Guardian

blocks.note: an observer watches
to dog someone is to keep following them

explanation.surface: How the Observer newspaper operates: by trailing its sister paper, the Guardian.
explanation.walkthrough: The Observer and the Guardian are sister British newspapers, but here they are lower-case ideas: one who observes, and a guardian.
explanation.definitionFit: A watchdog is a guard dog, or figuratively a body that guards against wrongdoing.

clue.text: Cable to our boss patiently worked on

blocks.note: coax is coaxial cable
ED is the editor, boss of the newspaper staff

explanation.surface: A telegram to the boss after a lot of careful work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Our boss' is the editor from the newspaper's point of view, the setter writing for a paper.
explanation.definitionFit: To coax someone is to persuade them gently and patiently, steadily working on them.

clue.text: A day good to be in

blocks.note: taken as written
Mon is the abbreviation for Monday
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: A fine day to stay indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the last word only; 'to be' links it.
explanation.definitionFit: Among and in are both prepositions for being situated within a group or surrounded by things.

clue.text: In St John's Island, head right to the end for air

indicators.note: the head is moved all the way to the back, so the front letter goes last

blocks.note: St John wrote Revelation on the Greek island of Patmos

explanation.surface: On an island, someone heads right to its far end for a breath of fresh air.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition gives ATMOSPHERE, which is entered with HERE removed. St John's sounds like a city, but it is the apostle's island of exile.
explanation.definitionFit: The atmosphere is the air surrounding the earth, or the air in a particular place.

clue.text: Caught with drink, one's beaten

blocks.note: snared means trapped or caught
rum is a drink

explanation.surface: Someone caught drinking is defeated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beaten' suggests a loser, but a drum is something you beat.
explanation.definitionFit: A snare drum is a percussion instrument struck with sticks, so it is one thing that gets beaten.

clue.text: Relative defends European views, not orthodox

indicators.note: a defender stands around what it protects, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: sis is short for sister
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A family member stands up for a European's unconventional opinions.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition gives HERESIES, entered with HERE removed.
explanation.definitionFit: Heresies are beliefs that contradict accepted doctrine, so they are opinions departing from orthodoxy.

clue.text: Don't reveal much at first — try to find out?

indicators.note: what comes at first is at the very start, so only the opening letter counts

blocks.note: the first letter of 'much'
to ask is to try to find something out

explanation.surface: Advice to a poker player or interviewee: give little away early, then probe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Much' is used only for its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To mask something is to hide or disguise it, keeping it from being revealed.

clue.text: Pour water on small tree

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small
an oak is a tree

explanation.surface: Watering a little sapling.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as gardening; the definition is the first three words.
explanation.definitionFit: To soak something is to drench it thoroughly with liquid, wetting it right through.

clue.text: See 7
One now not seen in pub, having gone missing, drunk?

definitions.text: One now not seen in pub

indicators.note: a drunk slurs words, so we want how the phrase comes out of a tipsy mouth

blocks.note: astray means gone missing; slurred as a drunk would say it, the S becomes SH

explanation.surface: A pub regular has wandered off, the worse for drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Gone missing is astray; slurred by a drunk, the S becomes SH. Smoking was banned in English pubs in 2007, so ashtrays vanished from them.
explanation.definitionFit: Since the smoking ban, ashtrays are no longer provided on pub tables, so this item is now absent there.
